overview.title: Adversarial examples and brittleness
overview.subsection: 19.1.2 Deep learning models are highly sensitive to phrasing and other distractors
overview.main_topic: Sensitivity of deep learning models to how their input is presented, illustrated by adversarial examples in vision
overview.central_idea: By gradient ascent in input space, an image can be changed imperceptibly so that a classifier changes its prediction (a panda becomes a 'gibbon'); this shows how brittle models are and how different their input-to-output mapping is from human perception. LLMs show an analogous sensitivity to small prompt changes.
overview.importance: It introduces the second limitation in section 19.1 and links it to a technique the reader already knows: the gradient ascent in input space used for filter visualization in chapter 10 (p.317).
learning_objectives: Explain how gradient ascent in input space produces an adversarial example, and how it relates to filter visualization
Explain what adversarial examples reveal about the gap between model and human perception
prerequisites: Gradients with respect to inputs and gradient ascent (chapter 10, p.317)

summary:
The page opens by finishing the point from p.590: patching failing prompts one by one does not address the general issue, and "even already patched prompts will still fail if you make small changes to them!"

Section **19.1.2** then introduces a closely related problem: deep learning models are extremely sensitive to *how* their input is presented. For image models the classic demonstration is the **adversarial example**: an input designed to trick the network into misclassifying it. The authors connect this to chapter 10: gradient ascent in input space can generate inputs that maximize the activation of a ConvNet filter, which is how filters were visualized (p.317).

The same idea, applied to the *class prediction* instead of a filter, gives adversarial examples. Starting from a picture of a panda, you add a small "gibbon gradient" (the gradient of the gibbon class score with respect to the input pixels) and the network now classifies the image as a gibbon. **Figure 19.3** shows this: the original panda image (predicted "Panda"), a noise-like "Gibbon class gradient" image, and the resulting "Adversarial example" that looks identical to the panda for a person but is predicted "Gibbon!". The small f(x) curves above the images stand for the model's output.

The authors draw two conclusions: these models are brittle, and their input-to-output mapping differs deeply from human perception.

The last paragraph starts the parallel for LLMs: they are extremely sensitive to minor prompt details, and innocuous changes such as changing place and people's names (continued on p.592) can significantly degrade performance.

paragraphs.excerpt: without addressing the more general underlying issue. Even already patched prompts will
paragraphs.what_it_says: Patching failing prompts one at a time does not address the underlying issue; a patched prompt fails again if you change it slightly.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The patch is a memorized correction for one point in input space. Nearby points (small rewordings) are not covered, because the model's general behavior has not changed.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It bridges 19.1.1 (novelty) and 19.1.2 (sensitivity to phrasing): small changes to the input can move the model off the patched point, which is exactly the sensitivity the next section describes.
connections: p.590: start of this sentence: LLM maintenance is a whack-a-mole game of patching failing prompts.

paragraphs.excerpt: A closely related problem is the extreme sensitivity of deep learning models
paragraphs.what_it_says: Deep learning models are extremely sensitive to how their input is presented. Image models are affected by adversarial examples, inputs designed to trick the network into misclassifying them. The reader already knows that gradient ascent in input space can generate inputs that maximize a ConvNet filter's activation; that was the basis of filter visualization in chapter 10.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A trained network is a differentiable function of its input, so you can compute how each pixel should change to increase any quantity inside the network. In chapter 10 the quantity was a filter's mean activation; you started from noise and climbed the gradient to see what pattern the filter responds to. The same machinery can be pointed at something you want to *fool*.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows that adversarial examples are not an exotic attack: they follow directly from the basic tools of deep learning (differentiability and gradients). Any differentiable model can be probed this way.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Training uses gradients with respect to the weights, $\nabla_W L$, with the input fixed. Filter visualization and adversarial examples use gradients with respect to the input, $\nabla_x$, with the weights fixed.

terminology.meaning: An input deliberately modified (often imperceptibly) so that a model makes a wrong prediction.
Repeatedly changing the input in the direction of the gradient of some target quantity (a filter activation, a class score) to increase it.

connections: p.317: section 10.2, visualizing ConvNet filters by gradient ascent in input space.
p.592: the LLM analogue: small prompt changes degrade performance.

paragraphs.excerpt: Similarly, through gradient ascent, you can slightly modify an image to maximize
paragraphs.what_it_says: Through gradient ascent you can slightly modify an image to maximize the prediction for a chosen class. Adding a 'gibbon gradient' to a panda picture makes the network classify it as a gibbon (Figure 19.3). This shows both the brittleness of these models and the deep difference between their input-to-output mapping and human perception.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In Figure 19.3 the panda image is fed to the model and predicted 'Panda'. The gradient of the gibbon score with respect to the pixels looks like colored noise; a small multiple of it is added to the panda. To a person the result is the same panda, but the model now says 'Gibbon!'. So the features the model relies on can be changed by perturbations far too small for humans to notice, and in a direction humans would never associate with 'gibbon'.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: If a perception system can be flipped by invisible changes, its notion of 'panda' is not the same as ours, even though it agrees with us on natural images. This is a practical security concern and a conceptual one: high test accuracy does not mean the model has learned human-like concepts. The book returns to this theme with the 'dim image in a mirror' of Figure 19.4 (p.594).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the famous panda/gibbon figure comes from Goodfellow, Shlens and Szegedy (2015), who used the 'fast gradient sign method' and a perturbation of size 0.007 per pixel (on a 0-1 scale). In high dimensions, many tiny per-pixel changes all aligned with the gradient add up to a large change in the class score, which is one explanation for why such small perturbations work.

terminology.meaning: The gradient of a class score (here 'gibbon') with respect to the input pixels; it tells how to change each pixel to increase that score.
Correct behavior that breaks under small, irrelevant changes of the input.

connections: p.594: Figure 19.4, models as a dim image of human concepts.
p.629: chapter 20 summary lists sensitivity to phrasing and distractors as a core limitation.

paragraphs.what_it_says: LLMs show an analogous, extremely high sensitivity to minor details in their prompts. Innocuous modifications such as changing place and people's names (sentence continues on p.592) can degrade performance.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The prompt plays the role of the image: changes that leave the meaning unchanged for a human can still move the input to a region where the model behaves differently.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It carries the vision example over to language models, which are the focus of the rest of the section (prompt engineering, p.592).

concepts.name: Adversarial example
concepts.definition: An input crafted, usually by a small perturbation, so that a model misclassifies it while a human sees no meaningful change.
concepts.intuition: A tiny nudge in exactly the direction the model is most sensitive to.
concepts.technical: Typically built by gradient ascent on a target class score (or descent on the true-class score) with respect to the input, under a bound on the perturbation size.
concepts.significance: Evidence that models' decision rules differ from human perception and can be exploited.
concepts.example: Figure 19.3: panda + small gibbon class gradient -> classified as gibbon.
concepts.misconception: That adversarial noise must be large or visible to work.

concepts.name: Gradient ascent in input space
concepts.definition: Modifying the input (not the weights) along the gradient of a chosen quantity in order to increase it.
concepts.intuition: Ask the model 'which way should each pixel move to make you more confident of X?', then move them.
concepts.technical: With weights fixed, compute $\nabla_x g(x)$ for a target $g$ (a filter activation or class logit) and update $x \leftarrow x + \eta\, \nabla_x g(x)$.
concepts.significance: The same tool drives filter visualization (chapter 10) and adversarial examples.
concepts.example: Starting from noise to visualize a filter (p.317), or starting from a panda to create a fake gibbon (this page).
concepts.misconception: That gradients are only used for training weights.

concepts.name: Brittleness / sensitivity to input presentation
concepts.definition: The tendency of deep learning models to change their output under small changes in how an input is presented, even when the meaning is unchanged.
concepts.intuition: The model's decision boundary passes very close to most natural inputs in some directions.
concepts.technical: Models fit a curve to the training data; off the data manifold, or along directions the training data never constrained, the function can vary sharply.
concepts.significance: It is limitation number two in section 19.1, and the reason for prompt engineering (p.592).
concepts.example: Adversarial images; LLM performance dropping when names or variable names change.
concepts.misconception: That robustness on the test set implies robustness to small perturbations.

math.title: Building an adversarial example by gradient ascent
math.source_text: By taking a picture of a panda and adding to it a gibbon gradient, we can get a neural network to classify the panda as a gibbon

variables.meaning: The original image (the panda), as a tensor of pixel values
The model's score (logit or log-probability) for the class 'gibbon' given input x
The 'gibbon class gradient': how each pixel should change to increase the gibbon score (middle image of Figure 19.3)
A small step size that keeps the change imperceptible
The adversarial example (right image of Figure 19.3)

math.operations: Compute the gradient of the target class score with respect to the input pixels (weights fixed), scale it by a small epsilon and add it to the image. This can be repeated for several steps.
math.purpose: Formalizes the book's verbal description of 'adding a gibbon gradient' to a panda.
math.interpretation: The gradient points in the direction of input space where the gibbon score rises fastest. Because images have very many pixels, a tiny change per pixel in that direction can produce a large change in the score.
math.intuition: Instead of changing the model to fit the data (training), you change the data to fit the answer you want.
math.numerical_example: Illustration (not from the book): suppose the gibbon logit is linear near $x$, $s(x) = w^\top x$, with $d = 150{,}528$ input values (a 224x224x3 image). Using the sign-of-gradient variant, $x_{adv} = x + \epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}(w)$, the logit increases by $\epsilon \sum_i |w_i|$. With $\epsilon = 0.007$ and an average $|w_i| = 0.01$, that is $0.007 \times 0.01 \times 150{,}528 \approx 10.5$ logits, enough to change the predicted class, while no pixel changed by more than 0.7%.

deeper.title: Same tool, three uses
deeper.body:
Gradients are used throughout the book in three ways:

| Use | What is fixed | What changes | Objective |
|---|---|---|---|
| Training (chapter 2) | input $x$ | weights $W$ | decrease the loss |
| Filter visualization (p.317) | weights $W$ | input $x$ (start from noise) | increase a filter's activation |
| Adversarial example (this page) | weights $W$ | input $x$ (start from a real image) | increase the score of a wrong class |

The last two differ mainly in the starting point and the target. Filter visualization asks what a unit *likes*; an adversarial example finds the *smallest* change to a real image that gets a wrong answer.

deeper.title: An optical-illusion analogy
deeper.body: Humans also have optical illusions, but they exploit regularities of our visual system and we can usually see that something is odd. Adversarial examples are different: the image is indistinguishable from the original to us, while the model's answer flips completely. That asymmetry is what the book means by 'the deep difference between their input-to-output mapping and our human perception.'

deeper.title: Why tiny changes add up
deeper.body: Beyond the book: one common explanation (Goodfellow et al., 2015) is that models behave fairly linearly in input space. For a linear score $w^\top x$, a perturbation $\delta$ with each entry at most $\epsilon$ in absolute value can change the score by up to $\epsilon\,\lVert w \rVert_1$, which grows with the number of input dimensions. A change of $\epsilon$ per pixel is invisible, but summed over ~150,000 pixels it can be decisive. See the numerical example in the math section.

misconceptions.claim: Adversarial examples require access to some bug in a specific model implementation.
misconceptions.correction: They follow from the model being a differentiable function: gradient ascent in input space, the same technique as filter visualization, is enough.

misconceptions.claim: The 'gibbon gradient' adds a faint picture of a gibbon to the panda.
misconceptions.correction: In Figure 19.3 the gradient looks like colored noise. It encodes the directions the model is sensitive to, not anything a human would recognize as a gibbon.

misconceptions.claim: A model with high test accuracy perceives images the way we do.
misconceptions.correction: The book uses adversarial examples as evidence of a deep difference between the model's input-to-output mapping and human perception.

prerequisites.note: Gradient ascent in input space for filter visualization.

related_code.note: The filter-visualization code computes gradients of an activation with respect to the input image; an adversarial attack is a small change of target.

related_figures.note: Figure 19.4: the gap between models and human mental models.

takeaways: Patched prompts still fail with small changes: patching does not address the general issue.
Deep learning models are highly sensitive to how inputs are presented; adversarial examples are the image-model case.
Adversarial examples are made by gradient ascent in input space, the same technique used for filter visualization in chapter 10, but aimed at a class score.
Figure 19.3: a panda plus a small 'gibbon class gradient' looks unchanged to people but is classified as a gibbon, showing brittleness and a mapping very different from human perception.
LLMs have the analogous problem with prompts: harmless changes such as names can degrade performance.

questions.question: Which technique from chapter 10 does the book say is the basis for creating adversarial examples?
options: Fine-tuning the top layers of a pretrained model
questions.explanation: The page reminds the reader that gradient ascent in input space was used to generate inputs maximizing a filter's activation (filter visualization) and that the same process aimed at a class prediction yields adversarial examples. Heatmaps visualize where a class is detected but don't create new inputs. Data augmentation and fine-tuning change the training process or the weights, not a test input.

questions.question: Describe the three images in Figure 19.3 and what the model predicts for each.
questions.answer: Left: the original panda photo, predicted 'Panda'. Middle: the gibbon class gradient (noise-like, with a gibbon photo below it indicating which class it targets). Right: the adversarial example (panda + gradient), which looks like the original panda but is predicted 'Gibbon!'.
questions.explanation: The figure shows that an imperceptible change in the image upends the classification, as the caption says.

questions.question: In training, filter visualization and adversarial example generation, what is held fixed and what is changed?
questions.answer: Training: input fixed, weights changed to reduce loss. Filter visualization: weights fixed, input changed (from noise) to increase a filter activation. Adversarial example: weights fixed, input changed (from a real image) to increase a wrong class's score, with a small perturbation.
questions.explanation: All three use gradients; the last two use gradients with respect to the input, which is why the book calls adversarial examples a direct consequence of the chapter-10 technique.

questions.question: What two conclusions does the book draw from the panda/gibbon example?
options: Models need more data and larger architectures
Models are brittle, and their input-to-output mapping differs deeply from human perception
Gibbons and pandas share visual features that humans miss
Adversarial examples only affect small models
questions.answer: Models are brittle, and their input-to-output mapping differs deeply from human perception
questions.explanation: The text says this 'evidences both the brittleness of these models and the deep difference between their input-to-output mapping and our human perception.' The book does not suggest that more data fixes this (p.595 argues scale does not). The perturbation is not a real shared feature. Nothing restricts the phenomenon to small models.

questions.question: A model's gibbon logit is approximately linear around an image, $s(x) = w^\top x$. You change every pixel by $\pm\epsilon$ following the sign of $w$. If the image has 10,000 pixel values, $\epsilon = 0.01$, and the average $|w_i|$ is 0.05, how much does the logit increase?
questions.explanation: Moving each coordinate by $\epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}(w_i)$ adds $\epsilon |w_i|$ to the score per coordinate. The sum over many dimensions is large even though each change is tiny. This is an AI-added illustration of why the imperceptible change in Figure 19.3 can flip the class.

questions.question: Can you explain, without notes, how the LLM sensitivity introduced at the bottom of this page is analogous to adversarial images?
questions.answer: In both cases a change that is irrelevant to a human (invisible pixel noise; different names or wording) moves the input to a different region of the model's input space, where the model behaves differently. The model does not respond to meaning as a human would.
questions.explanation: The page explicitly says 'Similarly, LLMs suffer from an extremely high sensitivity to minor details in their prompts,' and p.592 develops this with the Alice riddle and prompt engineering.
